newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Grain - Prices up in cat-mouse game.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Grain - Prices up in cat-mouse game.

text.p: Australia's cash grains market rose well in the past week with supply tight and a big buyer, the Australian Wheat Board (AWB), paying prices which had parts of the trade perplexed.
Last week's rises, in thin volume, left expectations on Friday that the coming week would produce a solid gain.
"I think activity will pick up," GrainCorp's Guy Allen said.

In a week when the AWB further increased its pool price, knocked back well-priced bids in its domestic wheat tender and confirmed that had full export order books until May, the biggest surprise for domestic traders was a price of A$165 a tonne which the AWB paid on Wednesday for Australian Standard White (ASW) wheat delivered Newcastle.

The price includes receivals charges and equates to about A$174 when these are taken into account, well ahead of the Sydney Futures Exchange (SFE) price of A$171 for the March 1997 contract the day before.
The AWB's purchase pushed March 1997 futures up by A$3 to A$175 on Thursday, leaving brokers surprised and concerned that the already-strong Australian market was heading too high.
Traders had speculated for months that the AWB was propping prices with a high pool price to keep world prices up.

The high cash market purchase last week deepened concern. The market was headed toward the upside, Brendan Hillary of ANZ Futures Ltd said on Thursday. The market was being "pushed around" by the high pool price and by the cash market, Chris Gray of C,A & L Bell Commodities said on Friday.
AWB had already surprised the market on Monday by increasing its pool price by A$1 to A$193 a tonne for ASW.

Bill Mitchell of New England Agricultural Traders (NEAT) said the "quite good" cash prices paid for wheat during the past week indicated the Sydney market was being squeezed. Shorts who were required to pay to exit had created the spike, he said.
But Chicago was also up, the AWB pools were still open, the cash market had firmed and there was a lack of readily available physical wheat on offer, he said.

Guy Allen of GrainCorp saw the rally based on light selling. The AWB, after raising its pool price, also passed over some aggressive bids, most notably A$171.50 for ASW Newcastle, in its latest domestic tender. This had bulled the market, Allen said.
The cash wheat market was hard to gauge because of light trade, Allen said. He saw cash wheat prices rising by A$5-A$6 over the week to A$170 bid Newcastle, with offers in the mid A$170s.
Australia's sorghum harvest, delayed slightly because of wet weather, was returning to normal, he said.
"I think it's all right," Mitchell also said. There would be some rain damage but reports were of a good crop, he said.
Sorghum values over the week dropped defensively before rising A$3-A$4 to return to about A$155 Newcastle.
The U.S. win of Pakistan business was good for world markets, Mitchell said. However, the trade was still watching for a re-entry of U.S. subsidies, another trade source said.
Settlement price gains for SFE wheat futures last week ranged from A$3.50 for May 1998 to A$14 for September 1998.
